63.history: The bay of hawks on the west coast, settled in the thousand two hundred and seventy-fourth year by three hill households too many for the grazing above Baile ghorm, the first hill-folk on that shore. They built round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and fished with lines and baskets from the shore and not from boats. Beathag, eldest of the crossing, walked the nine days on her own feet and was the first buried within sound of that tide. Flòraidh was born here, found amber in the wrack at nine, learned the drill from a blind drill-master, and carried the finest bead of the western strand the length of the island to lay it at the ford at the king's word. She married the boat-mender's son who followed her west, and was buried facing the water.

142.history: A green rise in the north-west where the settlements lived on seal, fish and deer until the thousand three hundred and seventy-ninth year, when small herds driven up Rathad na Spor by stages over three summers brought cattle there for the first time. The first calves born on the rise were watched through their first winter by the whole settlement in turn. It became the farm town of the north-west, and its hides went south by Rathad na Spor.
142.known_for: the first cattle of the north-west

476.history: A rise above the firth on the far western coast, where a long-house forty paces long, byre and hall under one roof, was raised in the thousand four hundred and sixteenth year, timbered from Rathad na Spor's own hills and roofed with turf. It was the greatest building of the age in the north-west and was spoken of the length of the coast. A spark from an untended hearth caught the byre-end thatch four years later and the hall burned with the byre; the household raised it again on the same footing before the next winter, holding the ground proved good whatever the fire proved of the roof, and left its scorch mark for anyone to see. It burned and was raised again once more before the age was out.

1.history: A settlement on the wide strait on the western coast where, in the thousand five hundred and sixty-second year, a household set a hollowed stone with seal oil and a wick of moss on its hearth-ledge and lit it: the first light on Dia-thìr that was not a hearth, giving little smoke. Within three winters every house on that stretch kept one burning through the dark months, and the lamps went along the coast with the seal-hunters.

191.history: A river-mouth on a wild strait where, in the thousand five hundred and ninety-eighth year, households staked a fence of woven wattle out into the ebb to trap salmon on the falling tide. The fence washed out twice before the third setting held, and the same line of stake-holes was fished again every year after through the rest of the age. Its smoked salmon went to Cruinneachadh an Àtha and along the coast road.

234.history: A settlement on a northern stream where cloth was first woven on standing frames, the warp held taut by weights of fired clay rather than by hand, in the thousand six hundred and twenty-eighth year; a worker stood free to pass the weft with both hands. Beitris was born into the third household to raise a frame here, and her blue-black cloth lay flatter and held its dye better than any other hand's. The king stopped at her stall at the ford, tested the weave with two fingers, and married her; she went south to Dùn ìseal and taught the standing weights to the hill's women until the craft had spread to a dozen sheds. The loom-weights lie in rows in the houses of the stream where they fell from the warp.

27.history: A settlement at the harbour mouth on Loch chrom, where in the thousand seven hundred and eighth year a young keeper cut marks for the high water on a boulder, at the interval of the first tide-rock, which he had never seen. The king stood before it with Beitris the better part of an afternoon and told her a thing can be worth doing before anyone has worked out why. The marks crept upward from keeper to keeper as the lake rose, a hand's width in a lifetime. Seònaid Mhòr cut her marks in pairs, for high water and low, and cut a last pair for the fosterling on the evening before he went home. By the two thousand four hundred and twenty-fifth year some sixty houses stood round the rock and An Cnoc Ruadh's stone landing, the greatest settlement on the shores of Loch chrom, its people fishing from boats of their own building.
27.known_for: the tide-rock and its rising marks
